notesStmt.note: According to Horace Traubel, Whitman sent these pages to his printers, the Ferguson Brothers, on February 23, 1891.

These pages are the copy text for the preface and opening poetry section of Good-Bye My Fancy (1891) that Whitman sent to the printer, to be set in type and printed as galley proofs. The pages of copy were enclosed in a paper folder and preceded by a note to the printer, both of which are included here.

div.p: My notion w'd be for you to put two compositors (among y'r best ones) on this, & set it all up complete ‸pp: 3 to 42 —& let me have the galley proofs complete, (I sh'd say five possibly six galleys)———

The measure is to be exactly the same as in "Nov. Boughs" set up by you ‸the additional pp: are to go in with the other book, bound in it —long primer—as before Horace Traubel is to manage &c: the same as myself.

div.head: Preface Note to 2d Annex,
concluding L of G—1891
div.p: Had I not better withhold (in this old age and paralysis of me) such little tags and fringe-dots (maybe specks, stains,) as follow a long dusty journey and witness it afterward? I have ‸probably not been ‸enough afraid of such ‸careless touches, from the first, ‸and am not now——nor of parrot-like repetitions,—as I grow older—nor even platitudes and the commonplace. (Perhaps I am too democratic for that ‸such avoidances.) Besides, is not the verse⹀field, as originally plann'd by my theory, ‸now sufficiently illustrated—with —and full time for me to now silently retire?—and(indeed amid no loud call or market for my sort of poetic utterance.)

¶ In answer, or rather defiance, to such ‸that kind of well⹀put questions interrogation, here comes a this little ‸volume cluster, and conclusion of all my preceding clusters. Though not at all clear that, as here collated, it is worth printing (certainly I have nothing fresh to write)—but am I neish?) I while away the hours of my 72d year—hours of
4
forced confinement in my den—first by putting in shape my this a last few ‸old⹀age very last old⹀age songs song⹀bits: small old age collation:
smaller type
Droplets Last droplets of and after spontaneous rain,
From many limpid distillations and
past showers;
(Will they all ‸they r all germinate anything? mere
exhalations ‸as they all are——the land's and sea's—
America's;
Will they filter to any deep emotion?
any heart and brain?)

¶ Anyhow However that may be, I will just feel to like improving to-day's opportunity ‸and wind⹀up. During the last two years and a half I have sent out, in the lulls of illness and paralysis ‸exhaustion, certain chirps—last and lingering⹀dying ones probably (undoubtedly)—which now I may as well ‸gather and, put in fair type while able to see correctly—(for my eyes plainly warn me they are dimming, and my brain more and more palpably neglects or refuses, month after month, even slight tasks or revisions.)

In fact, here I am these ‸current years 1889, and '90,90 and '91, (each successive month ‸fortnight week getting stiffer and stuck deeper) much like some hard⹀cased dilapidated grim ancient shell⹀fish or time⹀bang'd conch (no legs, utterly non⹀locomotive) cast ‸up high and dry on the ‸shore⹀sands, helpless to move or get anywhere—nothing left but behave
5
myself quiet, as possible, and while away the days yet assigned, and find discover if there is anything for the said grim and time⹀bang'd conch to be got at last out of born inherited good spirits and primal buoyant centre⹀pulses down there for deep somewhere within his gray⹀blurr'd old shell . . .4 em leaders . . . (Reader you must allow a little fun here—for one reason there are too many of the following poemets about
death, &c: and for another this day the time passing hours (July 5 1890,) is are so ‸sunny⹀fine—and old as I am I feel ‸to-day almost a part of some frolicsome wave, or for sporting yet like a kid or kitten—probably a streak of physical adjustment and perfection to-day. ‸here and now. I believe I have it all in me ‸perennially any how.)

div.p:
Then behind all, the ‸deep-down consolation (it is a glum one, but I dare not be sorry for the fact of it ‸in the past, nor refrain from dwelling, even vaunting here at the last end) that all this current late⹀years palsied old bodily shell⹀fish condition of me is the born indubitable outcome and growth, now ‸near for 20 18 years ‸along old of ‸too over⹀zealous, over⹀continued and too laborious bodily and emotional ‸excitement and action and excitement through the times of 1862, '3, '4 and '5 aiding and visiting and waiting⹀on ‸this later years, the ‸our wounded and sick army volunteers, both sides, ‸in campaigns or contests or after them, or in hospitals or fields south of Washington ‸city, or in that city place and elsewhere—those hot, sad,
6
determined wrenching ‸ times—the soldiers army volunteers, all States, ‸or North, or South——the wounded, suffering, dying—the hot exhausting ‸sweating summers, marches, battles, carnage—those trenches hurriedly heap'd by the corpse⹀thousands, mainly unknown—Will the America of the future—will this ‸vast rich Union ever realize
what itself cost, back there after all?—those hecatombs of mangled lives— battle⹀deaths—those times ‸and deaths of which, O far⹀off reader, this whole books is indeed finally ‸but a bit of ‸reminiscent memorial render'd by me from thence ‸by me to you?

head.hi: Sail out for good, Eidólon Yacht!

lg.l: Heave the anchor short!
Raise main-sail and jib—steer forth,
O little white-hull'd sloop, now speed on really deep waters,
(I will not call it our concluding voyage,
But outset and sure entrance to the truest, best, maturest;)

Depart, depart from solid earth—no more returning to these
shores,
Now on for aye our infinite free venture wending,
Spurning all yet tried ports, seas, hawsers, densities, gravitation,
Sail out for good, eidólon yacht of me!

lg.head: Lingering last drops.
lg.l: And when and why came you?
We know not wence whence, (was the answer,)

We only know that we drift here with
the rest,

That we linger'd and lagg'd—but were
wafted at last, and are now here,

To make for the passing shower's concluding
drops.

lg.head: Good bye my Fancy.
lg.l: Good bye* my fancy—(I had a word to say,

But ‸'tis not 'tis not quite yet the time‸has not arrived——The best of
any ‸man's word or say,
Is just when its proper place ‸arriveds—and for its meaning,
I keep mine for till the last.)
lg.note: * In ‸Behind a Good-bye there is lurks after all much of the salutation of ‸aanother beginning—to me continuity, dDevelopment, tTransformation, Continuity, Immortality ‸Transformation are the ‸chiefest life⹀meanings of Nature and Humanity, all and each, and are the si sine qua non of all ‸facts, and each, growth, advancement, fact.

lg.head: ON, ON THE SAME, YE JOCUND TWAIN!
lg.l: On, on the same, ye jocund twain!
My life and recitative, containing birth, youth, mid-age years,

Fitful as motley-tongues of flame, inseparably twined and
merged in one—combining all,

My single soul—aims, confirmations, failures, joys—nor sin-
glesingle
soul alone,

A strange eclaircissement of all the masses past, the eastern
world, the ancient, medieval,

Here, here from wanderings, strayings, lessons, wars, defeats—
here at the west a voice triumphant—justifying all,

A gladsome pealing cry—a song for once of utmost pride and
satisfaction;

I chant from it the common bulk, the general average horde,
(the best no sooner than the worst)—And now I
chant old age,

(My verses, written first for forenoon life, and for the summer's,
autumn's spread,

I pass to snow-white hairs the same, and give to pulses
winter-cool'd the same); ;)/

As here in careless trill, I and my recitatives, with faith and
love,
Wafting to other work, to unknown songs, conditions,
On, on, ye jocund twain! continue on the same!

lg.head: MY 71st YEAR.
lg.l: After surmounting three-score and ten,
With all their chances, changes, losses, sorrows,

My parents' deaths, the vagaries of my life, the many tearing
passions of me, the war of '63 and '4,

As some old broken soldier, after a long, hot, wearying march,
or haply after battle,

‸To-day At twilight, hobbling, answering yet to company roll-call, Here,
with vital voice,
Reporting yet, saluting yet the Officer over all.

lg.head: OLD AGE'S SHIP & CRAFTY DEATH'S.
lg.l: From east and west across the horizon's edge,
Two mighty masterful vessels sailers steal upon us:

But we'll make race a-time upon the seas—a battle-contest
yet! bear lively there!
(Our joys of strife and derring-do to the last!)
Put on the old ship all her power to-day!

lg.l:
Out challenge and defiance—flags and flaunting pennants
added,
As we take to the open—take to the deepest, freest waters.

Have I no weapon-word for thee—some message brief and
fierce?

(Have I fought out and done indeed the battle?) Is there no
shot left,
For all thy affectations, lisps, scorns, manifold silliness?
Nor for myself—my own rebellious self in thee?
Down, down, proud gorge!—though choking thee;
Thy bearded throat and high-borne forehead to the gutter;
Crouch low thy neck to eleemosynary gifts.

lg.head: The Pallid Wreath
lg.l: SOMEHOW I cannot let it go yet, funeral though it is,
Let it remain back there on its nail suspended,

With pink, blue, yellow, all blanc'd, and the white now gray
and ashy,
One wither'd rose put years ago for thee, dear friend,
But I do not forget thee. Hast thou then faded?
Is the odor exhaled? Are the colors, vitalities, dead?
No, while memories subtly play—the past vivid as ever;

For but last night I woke, and in that spectral ring saw
thee,
Thy smile, eyes, face, calm, silent, loving as ever:
So let the wreath hang still awhile within my eye-reach,
It is not yet dead to me, nor even pallid.

lg.head: An Ended Day.
lg.l:
The soothing sanity and blitheness of
completion,

The pomp and hurried ‸contest⹀glaze and rush
of day are done,
Now triumph! transformation! jubilate!*

note.seg: . . . . . . . In my rambles and explorations I found a woody place near the creek, that soon where for some reason the birds, in happy mood, seem'd to resort in unusual numbers.

Especially at the beginning of the day, and again at the ending. I was sure to find here— get there the most copious bird-concerts. I get I repair'd there frequently so at sunrise—and also at sunset, or just before . ‸. . . The Once, the question arose in me, Which is the best singing, the first or the lattermost? The first always exhilerated and perhaps seem'd more joyous and stronger; but I always felt the sunset or late afternoon sounds more penetrating and sweeter—seem'd to touch the soul—often the evening thrushes, two or three of them, responding and perhaps blending. ‸Though I miss'd some of the mornings, I found myself getting to be ‸quite strictly punctual at these evening utterances.

note.p: ‸Another Note.—"He went out with the tide, and the sunset," was a phrase I heard from a surgeon describing an old sailor's death under peculiarly gentle conditions.

During the Secession War, 1863 and '4, visiting the Army Hospitals ‸around Virginia— Washington, I soon early form'd the habit, and continued it to the end, whenever the ebb or flood tide began the latter part of day, of going to ‸punctually visiting those at that time populous wards ‸of suffering men. Somehow ‸(or I thought it so) the effect of the hour was palpable. The badly wounded would get some ease, and would like to talk a little, or be talk'd to. Intellectual and emotional natures would be at their best; deaths were always easier; medicines seem'd to have better effect when given then, and a lulling atmosphere would pervade the wards.
Similar influences, similar circumstances and hours, ‸day-close, after great battles, even with all their horrors. I had once or twice the same experience on the field covered with fallen or dead.

lg.head: SHAKSPERESHAKESPEARE-BACON'S CIPHER.
lg.l: I doubt it not—then more, far more;
In each old song bequeath'd—in every noble page or text,

(Different—something unreck'd before—some unsuspected
anuthor,)

In every object, mountain, tree, and star—in every birth and
life,

As part of each—finality of ‸evolv'd from each—meaning, behind the os-
tent,ostent,
The A mystic cipher waits infolded.

lg.head: TO THE SUN-SET BREEZE.
lg.l: Ah, whispering, something again, unseen,
Where late this heated day thou enterest at my window, door,
Thou, laving, tempering all, cool-freshing, gently vitalizing
Me, old, alone, sick, weak-down, melted-worn with sweat;

Thou, nestling, folding close and firm yet soft, companion bet-
terbetter
than talk, book, art,

(Thou hast, O Nature! elements! utterance to my heart be-
yondbeyond
the rest—and this is of them,)

So sweet thy primitive taste to breathe within—thy soothing
fingers on my face and hands,

Thou, messenger-magical strange bringer to body and spirit of
me,

(Distances balk'd—occult medicines penetrating me from head
to foot,)

I feel the sky, the prairies vast—I feel the mighty northern
lakes,

I feel the ocean and the forest—somehow I feel the globe
itself swift-swimming in space;

Thou blown from lips so loved, now gone—haply from end-
lessendless
store, God-sent,

(For thou art spiritual, Godly, most of all known to my
sense,)

Minister to speak to me, here and now, what word has never
told, and cannot tell,

Art thou not universal concrete's distillation? Law's, all As-
Astronomy'sAstronomy's
last refinement?
Hast thou no soul? Can I not know, identify thee?

lg.head: BRAVO, PARIS EXHIBITION! Exposition!
lg.l: Add to your show, dear before you close it, France,

With all the rest, visible, concrete, temples, towers, goods, ma-
chinesmachines
and ores,

Our sentiment wafted from many million heart-throbs, ethereal
but solid,

(We grand-sons and great-grand-sons do not forget your grand-
sires,)

From fifty Nations and nebulous Nations, compacted, sent
over-sea to-day,
America's applause, love, memories and good-will.
